content: Primary autoimmune haemolytic anaemia (AIHA) is a condition in which autoantibodies target and destroy red blood cells, leading to a variable disease course. Numerous immunomodulatory treatments have been used to manage this condition, but there is limited evidence to support their efficacy or to compare their effectiveness. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effects of different disease-modifying treatments in individuals with idiopathic AIHA. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including MEDLINE, Embase, LILACS, and the Cochrane Library, as well as clinical trial registries and conference proceedings. The search included records up to March 7, 2021, without any language restrictions. The analysis focused on randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared immunosuppressive or immunomodulatory treatments against no treatment, placebo, or other similar treatments in individuals of all ages with idiopathic AIHA. The primary outcomes of interest included complete haematological response at 12 months, frequency of adverse events at two, six, and 12 months, partial haematological response at 12 months, overall survival at six and 12 months, relapse-free survival (RFS) at six and 12 months, red blood cell (RBC) transfusion requirements at 12 months, and quality of life (QOL) as measured by validated instruments at 12 months. However, due to limited data availability, meta-analysis could only be performed for the frequency of complete haematological response. Two trials were included in the analysis, involving a total of 104 adult participants (96 randomized) with warm AIHA. Both studies were conducted in tertiary referral centers and compared the combination of rituximab and glucocorticoid therapy to glucocorticoid monotherapy. Rituximab was administered either as 375 mg/m² weekly for four weeks or as 1000 mg for two doses two weeks apart, while glucocorticoids were given as prednisolone at 1.5 or 1 mg/kg/day with tapering. The average age of participants in the two trials was 67 and 71 years, respectively. One of the studies demonstrated good methodological quality with a low risk of bias, while the other had a high risk of performance and detection bias due to the lack of blinding. The addition of rituximab to glucocorticoid therapy appeared to result in a significant increase in the rate of complete haematological response at 12 months compared to glucocorticoid monotherapy (96 participants; risk ratio [RR] 2.13; 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.34 to 3.40; low-certainty evidence). However, adverse event rates at the prespecified time points were not reported. Limited data were available on partial haematological response. The evidence regarding the effect of adding rituximab to glucocorticoids on partial haematological response at 12 months was highly uncertain (32 participants; one study; RR 3.00; 95% CI 0.13 to 68.57; very low-certainty evidence). Regarding RBC transfusion requirements at 12 months, one study reported that four participants in the rituximab group (mean number of packed red cell units: 4.0 ± 2.82) and five participants in the glucocorticoid-only group (mean number of packed red cell units: 5.6 ± 4.15) required transfusions. This indicated very uncertain evidence about the effect of adding rituximab to glucocorticoids (32 participants; RR 0.80; 95% CI 0.26 to 2.45; very low-certainty evidence). The other study did not report transfusion requirements at the prespecified time points but noted no significant difference in transfusion needs between the two groups when comparing responders from enrollment to the end of response or study follow-up (34 units versus 30 units; median [range]: 0 [1 to 6] versus 0 [1 to 5]; P = 0.81). Neither study explicitly reported overall survival or RFS rates at the prespecified time points. Additionally, no data on quality of life (QOL) were available. In conclusion, the current evidence on the effectiveness of immunomodulatory therapy for primary AIHA is limited to comparisons between rituximab plus glucocorticoid therapy and glucocorticoid monotherapy in patients with newly diagnosed warm AIHA. The findings suggest that the combination of rituximab and glucocorticoid may increase the rate of complete haematological response compared to glucocorticoid monotherapy. However, further studies are needed to provide more robust evidence and to evaluate other outcomes such as adverse events, survival rates, and quality of life.
